title: Strings
description: Storing text, joining it together, and the traps of adding numbers to it.

content.title: Anatomy of a String variable
content.caption: Declared exactly like the other types.

content.value: Why the capital S? `String` is not a primitive. It is a **class**, like your `Main` class. Java ships thousands of ready-made classes.
Capital letter means a class (`String`, `Main`). Lower case means a primitive (`int`, `double`, `boolean`, `char`).
content.title: Spot the difference

content.value: `+` joins text, left to right. Java adds nothing of its own, so every space must be inside the quotes.

content.value: If one side of `+` is text, Java turns the other side into text too. Between two numbers, `+` still adds. In a chain, the order decides.

content.title: Same numbers, different results
content.caption: Java works left to right. Once text enters the chain, every `+` after it joins.

quiz.question: Why is `String` written with a capital S when `int` is not?
options: `String` is a class, and every class name starts with a capital letter.
It is a mistake that Java never fixed.
Because text is more important than numbers.
quiz.explain: Primitive types are lower case; classes are capitalised. `String` is a class, which is also why a piece of text can do things like `length()`.

quiz.question: What does `System.out.println("Sum: " + 2 + 3);` print?
quiz.explain: Java works left to right. Once `"Sum: " + 2` has produced text, the `+ 3` joins on rather than adding. Brackets round `2 + 3` would give 5.

quiz.question: What does `System.out.println(2 + 3 + " total");` print?
quiz.explain: The chain starts with two numbers, so `2 + 3` is arithmetic and gives 5. Only after the text appears does `+` start joining.

quiz.question: What does `"Java".length()` give back?
quiz.explain: `length()` counts the characters in the text. Spaces count as characters too, so `"Pocket Lab".length()` is 10.

quiz.question: Which line is correct?
quiz.explain: A `String` value needs double quotes. Single quotes make a `char`, and Java will not quietly swap one for the other.
